title: Basie, bebop, rock and another sit-in story
summary: He did not like bebop or rock because it has no melody, and tells again of a union favor playing 'South Rampart Street Parade' with a rock band.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: You even know the commercial. Is that nice. Did -- did you hear Basie play with Walter Page. Do you know --
Basie? Count Basie?
Yeah.
Yeah. And --
What others, I heard what -- what I heard on the record player this morning when I came in that was -- sounded like some happy Germans playing some New Orleans --
Yeah. I don't know what she had on that record.
Some happy Germans playing some New Orleans music this morning. How about -- jazz, oh, after 1940, did you like Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker?
Well you see some of that music -- some of that music I didn't like at all, because I didn't know what they was playing --
Uh-huh.
No melody.
Uh-huh.
That's all that rock stuff, you know?
Uh-huh.
I like music, sure, but I can't get to like that rock business.
Uh-huh.
I turned down many jobs they want me to play. I say, Uh-uh. Why? I say, well there's no need for me to tell you a story, I just don't like that kind of music.
Uh-huh.
You know I wouldn't enjoy setting up there playing and don't enjoy. I like to en -- I enjoy my Playing as much as them people out there dancing or setting there listening.
Right. Right.
I enjoy it as much as you would or anybody else that's setting there listening to me playing.
So you like music that sings and swings.

I -- that's right, I just don't like that rock business, cause I don't know what I'm playing. I play it once, done the union a favor, one night they short of a bass player and they need a bass player and the business agent come over to me, ask, working tonight, I say no. He said man I want you to work. I said, with who? He told me

somebody, forget his name, who it was. I said 'Oh, no, I don't want to work.' 'Why man,' said, 'do me a favor,' said. 'Got to have somebody that's --' I said, 'well you know I don't like that kind of music, I don't like that playing with those guys, I don't know what they're playing.' 'Oh, men go there and do something, come on do that favor for me.' I said, 'no favor.' He kept on begging. I said, 'well all right, I'm tellyou I don't get my duty!' 'Well, a good man is a good titty,' he dall them titties, you know. I said, 'well I may be good, but I -- I said all right I'll do that favor for you.' I said 'don't come back no more and ask me to play for them.'

I went down there and I forget it was Washington, and LaBrea, not LaBrea, Washington and -- wherwas that at, in -- out on Washington Avenue. I went down there they was playing, I couldn't understand them. So they played a piece said, take one, bass. I take it -- see I'm (unintelligible) you understand, they can't get ahead of me. I -- tenor saxophone player -- he's boom-boom-boom-boom.

'Give the bass one' boom-boom- 'give him another one. Take another one, bass.' Boom-boom-that's all I played, I didn't know what he was doing -- so said man that was hot, when he went out. I said, what's the name of that thing he's playing I can't think of that number. It's South Rampart Street Parade, I said, Oh, yeah. I couldn't get that thing in my mind, I know it I couldn't think of it. Ain't this awful. 'South Rampart

Street Parade," and I didn't no more know what I was playing than the man in the moon. He told me "South Rampart Street Parade, They're some -- awful breaks in that thing. Yeah. I say, yeah. Fine. Well if a man was ever glad that job was over with. It was me. Um. "South Rampart Street Parade." I know what it is.
